hints: Focus on what hot, concentrated, acidified $\text{MnO}_4^-$ does to alkenes, it cleaves each $\text{C=C}$ completely to carbonyls and carboxylic acids.
Count carbons in M, it has only 9 carbons while L has 10, so one carbon must have been lost as $\text{CO}_2$ from a terminal $\text{C=CH}_2$ group.
Now map the three oxygenated carbons in M back to the two original double bonds, one ring $\text{C=C}$ must open to give a keto-acid chain and the side-chain $\text{C=C}$ must give the second ketone.
walkthrough:
**Find the unsaturation in L**

L is $\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{16}$. Think of it simply first.

Degree of unsaturation = $$\frac{2(10)+2-16}{2} = 3$$
That is perfect for one ring plus two $\text{C=C}$ bonds, a typical terpene pattern.

**Recall oxidative cleavage rules**

Hot, concentrated, acidified $\text{KMnO}_4$ breaks every $\text{C=C}$ apart.

Useful summary: $$\text{R}_2\text{C=CR}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{ R}_2\text{C=O}$$ $$\text{R}_2\text{C=CH}_2 \rightarrow \text{R}_2\text{C=O} + \text{CO}_2$$ $$\text{RCH=CHR} \rightarrow 2\text{ RCOOH (via aldehydes)}$$

**Analyse product M**

M is $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH(COCH}_3\text{)CH}_2\text{COOH}$.

Count it, it is a $\text{C}_9$ molecule with two ketones and one carboxylic acid. Since we started with $\text{C}_{10}$ and got $\text{C}_9$, one carbon was lost as $\text{CO}_2$. That tells you L must contain a $\text{C=C(CH}_3\text{)CH}_2$ type terminal alkene, not an internal $\text{CH=CHCH}_3$ group.

**Rebuild L from M**

The $\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$ end and the central $\text{CH(COCH}_3\text{)}$ come from opening the methyl-substituted cyclohexene ring. The left $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_2$ end comes from the same ring opening.

Only 1-methyl-4-(prop-1-en-2-yl)cyclohex-1-ene, limonene, has both a trisubstituted ring $\text{C=C(CH}_3\text{)}$ and a terminal side-chain $\text{C(CH}_3\text{)=CH}_2$ in exactly the right positions to join up to give M on double cleavage.

options.A: This is limonene, 1-methyl-4-(prop-1-en-2-yl)cyclohex-1-ene. It has formula $\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{16}$, one ring and two C=C bonds. The terminal $\text{C(CH}_3\text{)=CH}_2$ cleaves to $\text{CH}_3\text{CO-}$ plus $\text{CO}_2$, accounting for the C10 to C9 loss, and the ring $\text{(CH}_3\text{)C=C}$ cleaves open to give the keto-acid chain seen in M.
options.B: The side chain here is $\text{-CH=CHCH}_3$, an internal alkene, not a terminal $\text{=CH}_2$. On vigorous oxidation this would cleave to give ethanoic acid ($\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$) after oxidation of ethanal, not the $\text{-COCH}_3$ ketone fragment required in the centre of M. It also would not lose carbon as $\text{CO}_2$ in the same way.
options.C: Although this has the correct terminal $\text{C(CH}_3\text{)=CH}_2$ side chain, the ring double bond is in the wrong place (cyclohex-2-ene pattern rather than 1-methylcyclohex-1-ene). Cleavage there would put the $\text{-CH}_2\text{COOH}$ and ketone fragments in different positions along the chain and would not give the 3-acetyl-6-oxoheptanoic acid skeleton of M.
options.D: This structure has two double bonds in the six-membered ring plus one side-chain double bond, giving degree of unsaturation 4. Its formula would be $\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{14}$, not $\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{16}$, so it is ruled out by molecular formula. Its side chain is also $\text{-CH=CHCH}_3$, which would not give the required methyl ketone plus $\text{CO}_2$ pattern.
